sessions.teaser: The group explored journaling through personal challenges, mindful breathing, and a story discussion. An emoji game lifted the energy.
sessions.fullSummary:
SECTION 1 — OVERVIEW
Meeting Objective: To conduct a structured learning session on the topic of journaling, including member challenge presentations, a breathing exercise, an interactive game, and a motivational story discussion, as part of an ongoing youth development program.
Total Meeting Duration: 1 hour 45 minutes 11 seconds
Host / Facilitator: ELF (primary host and session facilitator); SAHN / SAHN 2 (supervisor/mentor providing guidance and conducting the interactive game segment); BC (Ms. BCDF — thought-for-the-day presenter)
Participant Roles:
- ELF — Session host and facilitator
- SAHN / SAHN 2 — Program supervisor and mentor
- BC (Ms. BCDF) — Guest presenter (thought for the day)
- JFP — Member presenter and active contributor
- Kyla — Member presenter, active contributor, and boot camp commander
- BLC (BL2P / BLCOP) — Member presenter and next-week material provider
- alwe (Ali) — Member presenter and contributor
- Jayden — Member contributor and participant
- BC — Observer/contributor
Overall Engagement Level: Medium
Overall Sentiment: Mixed — predominantly positive with moments of confusion and low energy
Notable Dynamics: Participation was uneven, with Kyla and BLC being the most articulate contributors. Ali struggled with language clarity throughout. The interactive emoji-country guessing game significantly boosted energy and engagement. Attendance numbers were noted as declining, which was flagged as a concern.
Session Effectiveness Score: 6/10 — The session covered its intended topic thoroughly and included creative elements such as the breathing exercise, challenge presentations, and an interactive game. However, communication barriers, declining attendance, and inconsistent engagement among members reduced overall effectiveness.
---
SECTION 2 — KEY DISCUSSIONS & TOPICS
Introduction to Journaling
The session opened with ELF welcoming members and initiating a discussion on the day's topic: journaling. ELF began by asking participants to share their understanding of what journaling means, framing the exercise as an open, judgment-free discussion where there were no wrong or right answers. This approach was deliberate and effective in encouraging even less confident speakers to contribute.
Key discussion points:
Kyla was the first to respond, offering a clear and concise definition by describing journaling as "pouring your thoughts into an external form, like through a book," and characterizing it as a way of channeling one's inner world outward. Ali followed with a more fragmented but sincere response, describing journaling as a way of bringing out one's day and feelings about one's story. BLC then contributed a more structured definition, explaining that journaling involves expressing thoughts and feelings in various forms — whether in a physical book or typed digitally — and that it could serve as a recollection of events or a summary of one's emotional state. JFP added that journaling is a tool for writing down feelings and daily events, and that many people use it to keep track of and even control their emotions.
Insights or decisions:
ELF synthesized all contributions into a comprehensive summary, describing journaling as a way of creating a private space for self-reflection and emotional processing. ELF used the metaphor of "dumping all your stress, your happiness, and all other emotions into a piece of paper," explaining that this act of expression — even without an audience — can make one feel lighter and more in control. ELF further emphasized that journaling helps identify patterns in daily life and supports personal growth and self-improvement.
Questions addressed:
No formal questions were raised during this segment, but ELF's facilitation prompted each member to articulate their understanding, effectively turning the introduction into a collaborative definition-building exercise.
---
Scoreboard Review and Group Announcements
Following the journaling introduction, ELF presented a review of the previous week's session performance, covering attendance, challenge submissions, scores, and behavioral guidelines.
Key discussion points:
ELF noted that the previous session lasted 90 minutes and covered the topic of "sensing," with JFP serving as host. The members who attended were BLC, Gianni, Kyla, Ali, and Luna. ELF then shared individual scores: JFP scored 7.3, BLC scored 7.5, Gianni scored 6.6, Kyla scored 6.5, Ali scored 5.4, and Luna scored 1.4 — the lowest, attributed to non-submission of challenges. ELF also presented sentiment data from the previous session, noting that 38% of the session was positive, 30% neutral, 12% negative, and 20% mixed, expressing concern about the relatively high neutral and negative proportions.
Insights or decisions:
ELF highlighted a declining trend in participation numbers and explicitly tasked all members with inviting more people to join future sessions. The group was also reminded of the standing rule prohibiting discussion of politics, gender, or religion in any form — verbal or written — during sessions. ELF also noted that members were performing well in terms of asking quality questions, as evidenced by the question-and-answer bubble chart, but encouraged them to ask even more questions going forward.
Questions addressed:
No direct questions were raised during this segment, though ELF's announcements prompted acknowledgment from Kyla and other members.
---
Breathing Exercise
ELF transitioned the session into a breathing exercise, inviting Ali to lead the group through the activity. This was Ali's first time leading a breathing exercise, and the segment served both as a mindfulness activity and a leadership development opportunity.
Key discussion points:
Ali began the exercise somewhat abruptly and at a fast pace, prompting ELF to intervene and ask him to slow down, humorously noting that "you're not doing the Formula 1 race." After several corrections and restarts, Ali successfully guided the group through a basic box-breathing pattern: breathing in for a count of five, holding for three counts, and breathing out for five counts, repeated three times.
Insights or decisions:
Following the exercise, SAHN provided constructive feedback to Ali, advising that in future exercises, the leader should first ask participants to sit in a relaxed position and prepare themselves before beginning. SAHN also recommended that the leader give clear verbal instructions before starting — explaining the count structure in advance — and that the leader should personally perform the breathing alongside the group rather than simply narrating it.
Questions addressed:
Ali asked how long the exercise would be before beginning, which ELF addressed by redirecting him to start the exercise. SAHN's post-exercise feedback effectively addressed the gaps observed during the activity.
---
Weekly Challenge Presentations
The core of the session involved four members presenting their weekly challenges, all of which were centered on the theme of journaling. Each presenter shared their personal journaling experience, followed by a question-and-answer segment.
Key discussion points:
JFP's Presentation: JFP described completing the "Inner Explorer" challenge, which required writing three pages of unfiltered morning thoughts upon waking for three consecutive days. On day one, JFP's mind felt messy and scattered, filled with school-related worries and random thoughts. By day two, thoughts were more mixed but clearer, with some positive self-motivating ideas emerging. By day three, JFP reported feeling calmer, more organized, and more confident, with a shift from worry-based thinking to action-oriented planning. JFP concluded that journaling helped articulate thoughts more clearly and that treating it as a tool for self-improvement rather than a chore made it more sustainable.
Kyla's Presentation: Kyla also completed the "Inner Explorer" challenge and shared a summarized version of her morning pages. Her journal entry was written on her 15th birthday (April 3rd), capturing the excitement and mild panic of waking up at 5 AM to prepare for a birthday party she had only officially announced to friends the day before. Kyla described planning to make a matcha strawberry mille crepe cake and Japanese curry from her aunt's recipe, driven by a desire to serve something special made with love rather than something expensive. The entry also reflected on the passage of time, with Kyla noting that three years remained until she graduated and became an adult, and expressing a bittersweet nostalgia for childhood alongside excitement for the future.
BLC's Presentation: BLC took a unique approach to the challenge, writing three pages of morning pages based on a single vivid and surreal dream experienced the night before. The dream involved standing on a pier over a sea of liquid mercury, boarding a train that ran on a line of light, and finding the carriage filled with people BLC had lost contact with — all reading newspapers written in symbolic language. BLC sat next to an older version of themselves who handed them a warm stone. BLC's journaling process involved attempting to decode the dream's meaning, describing the sensory details of the dreamscape, and ultimately arriving at a personal reflection: the dream felt like a nudge to examine how BLC was handling personal growth, with the warm stone symbolizing the lessons carried from past experiences.
Ali's Presentation: Ali described a different approach to the challenge, writing about strange and imaginative thoughts that came to mind after waking up — inspired by content encountered on YouTube. Day one featured a scenario involving Socrates walking around Jogja (Yogyakarta); day two involved imagining what Marie Curie would be like if she were alive today; and day three featured Mario Bros becoming an F1 racer. Ali noted that this type of creative, unconstrained writing was enjoyable and that YouTube had suggested such exercises could enhance creativity.
Insights or decisions:
Across all four presentations, a consistent theme emerged: journaling — whether structured or free-form, dream-based or reality-based — consistently produced a sense of clarity, emotional relief, and self-awareness. The variety of approaches demonstrated that journaling is highly personal and adaptable, reinforcing ELF's earlier point that there is no single correct way to journal.
Questions addressed:
Multiple questions were raised during the Q&A segments following each presentation, which are documented in detail in Section 4.
---
Interactive Game: Guess the Country by Emoji (SAHN's Activity)
SAHN conducted a 10-minute interactive game in which participants were shown emoji combinations and asked to guess the corresponding country name. The activity served as an energy booster and a quick-thinking exercise.
Key discussion points:
The game covered a wide range of countries including Belgium, Germany, France, Poland, Iceland, China, Spain, Japan, Cuba, Finland, Thailand, Singapore, Ukraine, Oman, Portugal, Romania, Canada, Taiwan, Mali, Tonga, Denmark, Ireland, Greenland/Greece, Uruguay, Chile, Maldives, Sweden, Turkey, New Zealand, Kuwait, India, and Qatar. Participants competed enthusiastically to guess each answer, with BLC and Kyla emerging as particularly quick and accurate guessers. SAHN added an educational layer by occasionally asking for the capital cities of correctly identified countries, such as Helsinki for Finland, Ottawa for Canada, and Kyiv for Ukraine.
Insights or decisions:
The game was notably effective in raising the group's energy level and encouraging participation from members who had been quieter during the earlier segments. SAHN closed the activity by promising that similar games would be incorporated into future weekly sessions, which was met with enthusiasm from participants.
---
Thought for the Day: Story of "The Monkeys and the Bell"
Ms. BC (BCDF) presented a motivational video featuring an animated story called "The Monkeys and the Bell," framed within a conversation between two characters, Tia and Tofu, about overcoming fear.
Key discussion points:
The story followed a robber who stole a bell from a temple, only to be killed by a tiger attracted by the bell's sound. The bell was then found and played with by monkeys, causing villagers to believe an evil spirit was responsible. A brave woman investigated the truth, discovered the monkeys, lured them away with food, retrieved the bell, and was rewarded by the king. The moral of the story was that one must not be afraid of trifles, and that intelligence and courage succeed against all odds.
Insights or decisions:
Following the video, BC facilitated a structured discussion in which BLC, Kyla, Ali, Jayden, and JFP each contributed reflections. Kyla connected the story to her own experience of overcoming nervousness before a presentation, noting that she chose to proceed despite fear of judgment. JFP reflected that the story taught the importance of gathering facts before reacting to fear, and shared a personal anecdote about being afraid of crocodiles in a park before realizing trained guards were present. Ali summarized the lesson as "we cannot just say it straight away — we have to know the facts first." BLC reflected on the robber's story as a lesson in gratitude and contentment, arguing that greed and the desire for more than one already has can lead to negative consequences.
---
Boot Camp Updates and Announcements
In the final segment, ELF and members discussed upcoming boot camp activities and administrative updates.
Key discussion points:
ELF reminded all members who had not yet registered for the hybrid boot camp to do so as soon as possible. Kyla, who had been assigned as boot camp commander for her region, shared that she had already begun recruiting friends to participate and asked a clarifying question about the structure of Day 3 activities. JFP provided an overview of the planned boot camp structure: Day 1 would involve a community challenge in Singapore where participants would give muffins to elders and learn their stories; Day 2 would focus on innovation and creativity, imagining Singapore in 2040 and identifying personal traits and commitments; Day 3 would be a festival-style event with three games. ELF also announced that Ratna would be the host for the following week's session and that BLC had been assigned as the material provider for that session.
Insights or decisions:
BLC was asked directly whether they would attend the boot camp session that evening and gave an uncertain response, prompting ELF to request a clear yes or no reply via the group chat. ELF also reminded BLC to respond to messages and provide materials on time.
---
SECTION 3 — CHAT BOX SUMMARY
The chat box during this session served as a meaningful supplementary channel, with several participants using it to share reminders, personal reflections, questions, and humorous anecdotes that enriched the verbal discussion.
Boot Camp Registration Reminder:
One of the most practically significant chat contributions came from Kyla, who sent a direct message to BLC and JFP reminding them that the group needed to recruit more people to register for the hybrid boot camp in the region. This message was sent during the session and was acknowledged verbally by ELF, who thanked Kyla and noted that the reminder would be addressed at the end of the session. This proactive behavior demonstrated Kyla's sense of responsibility and awareness of group-level goals beyond the immediate session agenda.
Ali's Question for JFP:
Ali posted a question in the chat directed at JFP following his challenge presentation: "After you have good results, we wonder what obstacles will come up when you continue this habit." This was a thoughtful, forward-looking question that went beyond the surface-level discussion of journaling outcomes and probed the sustainability of the habit. While this question was not verbally addressed in the session, it reflected Ali's genuine curiosity and engagement with the topic, and it added a layer of depth to the discussion about journaling as a long-term practice rather than a short-term exercise.
Ali's Admission of a Challenge Mistake:
During Kyla's presentation, Ali posted in the chat: "WAIT ah..... I wrong work the weekly challenge." This candid admission suggested that Ali may have misunderstood the challenge requirements and completed a different task than intended. While this was not addressed verbally in detail, it provided context for why Ali's presentation took a more creative and unconventional approach — writing about imaginative scenarios rather than personal morning reflections. This chat message humanized Ali's experience and highlighted the importance of clear communication of challenge instructions.
BLC's Question for JFP (Pre-verbal):
BLC posted a question in the chat before asking it verbally: "JFP, had you found any correlation between the thoughts you had before you were asleep and in the morning? It's said that those thoughts before bed may influence our dreams and thoughts." This was one of the most intellectually substantive questions of the session, drawing on psychological knowledge about the relationship between pre-sleep cognition and dream content. BLC subsequently asked this question verbally, and JFP confirmed that there was indeed a correlation, noting that random "shower thoughts" before bed seemed to produce equally random and vivid dreams.
Ali's "Lucid Dream?" Comment:
During BLC's presentation about his dream-based journaling, Ali posted "Lucid dream?" in the chat, which prompted BLC to address the concept verbally. BLC confirmed that the dream was partially lucid — he had some control over his dialogue but not over his physical movements or actions. This single-word chat contribution effectively steered the conversation into an interesting and educational direction about the nature of lucid dreaming.
Ali's Moral Reflection:
During the thought-for-the-day discussion, Ali posted: "We can't just say it straight away, we have to know the facts first." This message captured the core moral of the story succinctly and was later echoed in Ali's verbal response when BC called on him to share his takeaway. The chat message demonstrated that Ali was actively processing the story's lesson even before being asked to speak.
Ali's Humorous Personal Anecdote:
In one of the most entertaining chat contributions of the session, Ali shared a personal story related to the theme of courage and not being afraid: "I have a little bit kinda funny experience so the toilet near my class. They say if you press the light switch you'll get electrocuted. Me a very very super super zuper brave people said 'ok lemme check if it can make a electrocuted I will prank my friend if not I will become the +100000000000000000000000000000000000000 aura people' and when I check jrek krek jrek its normal but the lamps not on but now I have a +10000000000000000000000000000000000000 aura." This message, while humorous and informal, was directly relevant to the session's theme of courage and fact-finding over fear, and it demonstrated Ali's creative and playful personality. It also showed that Ali was connecting the session's content to his own lived experience, which is a meaningful form of engagement.
Birthday Celebration Messages:
Several participants posted birthday wishes for Kyla in the chat, including "Selamat ulang tahun kami ucapkan" (Happy birthday to you in Bahasa Indonesia/Malay) and "Celebrate with fireworks 🎇." Kyla responded with "Selamat ulang tahun" to teach the group the phrase, and later posted "Thank you everyone, I appreciate it." These exchanges, while social in nature, contributed to a warm and inclusive group atmosphere and reinforced the sense of community within the group.
---
SECTION 4 — QUESTIONS BY PARTICIPANT
Kyla's Question to JFP
During the Q&A segment following JFP's challenge presentation, Kyla asked a reflective and insightful question: "What did you learn from journaling, and what helped you to improve yourself day after day?" This question was asked after Kyla observed that JFP's journal entries showed a clear progression from a messy, anxious mindset on day one to a calm, organized, and confident mindset by day three. Kyla was essentially probing the mechanism behind this improvement — not just what changed, but why and how. JFP responded by explaining that journaling helped him articulate his thoughts more clearly and that reframing the activity as a tool for self-improvement rather than a chore made it easier to sustain and more impactful. This was one of the most substantive exchanges of the session, as it moved the discussion beyond description and into the realm of metacognition and habit formation.
Jayden's Question to JFP
Jayden asked JFP a hypothetical question: "If your mind on day one was not messy when you woke up, would the outcome on day three be the same, or would it change?" This question was somewhat abstract and required clarification, but it touched on an interesting point about whether the journaling process itself drives improvement or whether the starting emotional state determines the trajectory. JFP responded by noting that his thoughts became more positive as the days progressed and that his stress and worries decreased, implying that the journaling process itself contributed to the improvement regardless of the starting point. While the exchange was brief, Jayden's question demonstrated a genuine attempt to think critically about the relationship between initial conditions and outcomes.
BLC's Question to JFP
BLC asked JFP a psychologically informed question: "Had you found any correlation between the thoughts you had before you were asleep and in the morning? It's said that those thoughts before bed may influence our dreams and thoughts." This question was first posted in the chat and then asked verbally, reflecting BLC's preparation and intellectual curiosity. JFP confirmed that there was indeed a correlation, noting that random pre-sleep thoughts — what the internet calls "shower thoughts" — seemed to produce equally random and vivid dreams. This exchange introduced a scientific dimension to the journaling discussion, connecting the practice to broader concepts of sleep psychology and cognitive processing.
BLC's Question to Kyla
BLC asked Kyla two related questions during her challenge presentation Q&A. The first was: "Before you started journaling, did you have any procrastination, and what were your initial thoughts about journaling?" Kyla responded honestly, admitting that she initially thought journaling would be boring and that she was not a "writing type person." However, she found that journaling became a space for releasing thoughts — treating the paper as a friend — and that it also served as a place to practice her language skills. BLC's follow-up question was: "Did your thoughts at the beginning remain valid when you saw the outcome?" This was a nuanced question about cognitive consistency — whether Kyla's initial skepticism was confirmed or overturned by the experience. Kyla's response was brief but affirmative, suggesting that her initial concerns were addressed through the process.
Ali's Question to BLC
Ali asked BLC a question about the creative and cognitive benefits of journaling: "Are activities like this — can they make us more creative / proactive?" The question was initially unclear due to language barriers, and BLC helped clarify the intended word ("proactive" or "creative"). Once understood, BLC gave a thoughtful response, explaining that journaling — especially when based on dreams or unusual thoughts — can stimulate imagination and creativity by encouraging the brain to find reasons, patterns, and outcomes for abstract or strange experiences. BLC noted that the more unusual the dream or thought, the more creative the process of decoding it becomes.
Jayden's Question to BLC
Jayden asked BLC two questions about his dream-based journaling experience. The first was: "When you woke up from that dream, did you feel shocked or nervous, and could you control your body in the dream, or were you frozen?" BLC responded that upon waking, he felt mysterious and somewhat shocked but not nervous. Regarding control within the dream, BLC explained that it was partially a lucid dream — he could control his dialogue but not his physical movements or actions. This response prompted Ali to post "Lucid dream?" in the chat, which BLC confirmed and elaborated on, noting that he had experienced fully lucid dreams before but that this particular dream was only partially lucid.
Kyla's Question to Ali
During Ali's challenge presentation Q&A, Kyla asked Ali: "What kind of weird things did you write about, and were they in Indonesian or English?" Ali clarified that his entries included scenarios like Socrates walking around Jogja and Mario Bros becoming an F1 racer — imaginative, impossible scenarios inspired by YouTube content. He confirmed that the entries were written in Indonesian (Bahasa Indonesia). Kyla also asked about the length of each entry, and Ali explained that the pages varied in length, with some being shorter and others containing around five words per line.
Jayden's Question to Ali
Jayden asked Ali: "Where did you write — in a special book, normal paper, or something else?" Ali responded that he used a thin book. This was a simple but practical question that grounded the discussion in the physical reality of journaling practice, reminding participants that the medium matters and that even a basic notebook is sufficient for the exercise.
BLC's Question to the Group (via JFP's facilitation)
During the thought-for-the-day discussion, JFP — prompted by BC — posed a question to BLC on behalf of the group: "In the story, the robber had high expectations but failed because he did something wrong — stealing the bell. How does this apply to our daily lives, and what can we do to prevent similar situations?" BLC responded thoughtfully, arguing that the robber's downfall was rooted in greed and a failure to appreciate what he already had. BLC suggested that the lesson is to validate one's current position, be grateful for existing resources, and avoid being driven by excessive desire for more. This response connected the story's moral to a broader life philosophy of contentment and ethical decision-making.
---
SECTION 5 — SENTIMENT & ENGAGEMENT BY PARTICIPANT
ELF: Sentiment: Positive | Engagement: High | Shifts: Showed mild frustration when members were slow to respond or gave unclear answers, but consistently maintained an encouraging and patient tone throughout the session.
SAHN / SAHN 2: Sentiment: Positive | Engagement: High | Shifts: None observed. Consistently supportive, constructive, and energizing — particularly during the breathing exercise feedback and the emoji game segment.
Kyla: Sentiment: Positive | Engagement: High | Shifts: Noticeably elevated energy and warmth during the birthday celebration segment. Remained consistently engaged and articulate throughout all discussion segments.
JFP: Sentiment: Positive | Engagement: Medium | Shifts: Experienced technical difficulties (Zoom connectivity issues) that caused intermittent disengagement. When present and connected, contributions were thoughtful and relevant.
BLC: Sentiment: Mixed | Engagement: Medium-High | Shifts: Demonstrated high intellectual engagement during presentations and Q&A, but showed hesitation and uncertainty during the boot camp commitment discussion, reflecting some ambivalence about participation.
alwe (Ali): Sentiment: Positive | Engagement: Medium | Shifts: Struggled with language clarity throughout, which occasionally reduced the impact of contributions. However, chat messages revealed genuine engagement and humor, suggesting higher internal engagement than was verbally apparent.
Jayden: Sentiment: Positive | Engagement: Medium | Shifts: Became noticeably more energized and participatory during the emoji game. Verbal contributions during discussions were limited but present.
BC (Ms. BCDF): Sentiment: Positive | Engagement: Medium | Shifts: None observed. Fulfilled a specific role (thought-for-the-day presenter) and engaged warmly with participants during the story discussion.
Sentiment Summary:
- Positive: 65%
- Mixed: 20%
- Neutral: 15%
- Negative: 0%
---
SECTION 6 — OPEN ACTIONS & FOLLOW-UPS
- All members to invite new participants to future sessions to address declining attendance (Due: Ongoing)
- BLC to confirm boot camp attendance via group chat (Due: Same day as session)
- BLC to prepare and submit session materials for next week (Due: Before next Saturday session)
- Kyla / any member to inform Ratna that she is the host for next week's session (Due: ASAP)
- All unregistered members to register for the hybrid boot camp (Due: ASAP)
- All members to avoid discussing politics, gender, or religion in sessions or group chats (Due: Ongoing)
---
SECTION 7 — SESSION EFFECTIVENESS: STRENGTHS & IMPROVEMENTS
Strengths
- Diverse session structure: The session successfully combined multiple formats — open discussion, individual presentations, Q&A, a mindfulness exercise, an interactive game, and a motivational story — keeping the session varied and multi-dimensional.
- Strong facilitation by ELF: ELF maintained consistent energy, redirected off-track moments, and ensured all members had opportunities to contribute.
- High-quality challenge presentations: JFP, Kyla, and BLC delivered particularly thoughtful and well-articulated presentations that generated meaningful discussion.
- SAHN's game segment was a standout moment that dramatically increased group energy and participation, demonstrating the value of incorporating play into learning sessions.
- Inclusive atmosphere: The birthday celebration for Kyla and the multilingual interactions created a warm, community-oriented environment.
Areas for Improvement
- Declining attendance is a structural concern that needs to be addressed proactively through member recruitment and retention strategies.
- Language barriers — particularly for Ali — reduced the clarity and impact of his verbal contributions. Providing language support or allowing bilingual responses could help.
- Ali's challenge misunderstanding suggests that challenge instructions need to be communicated more clearly and confirmed before the session.
- Boot camp communication was unclear and last-minute for some members (notably JFP), indicating a need for better advance notice and follow-through on Telegram messages.
- Q&A facilitation could be more structured — some question-and-answer exchanges were cut short or went unaddressed due to time or connectivity issues.
---
SECTION 8 — ENGAGEMENT SCORE
ELF: Score 8/10 — Consistently active as facilitator, managed transitions smoothly, corrected Ali's breathing exercise with patience and humor, and kept the session on track despite connectivity issues and uneven participation. Could improve by allowing more organic discussion time.
SAHN / SAHN 2: Score 9/10 — Provided high-value mentorship feedback on the breathing exercise, delivered an energizing and well-received interactive game, and maintained a positive and encouraging presence throughout. A model contributor for the session.
Kyla: Score 8/10 — Delivered a personal, well-structured, and emotionally resonant challenge presentation. Asked a high-quality question to JFP and actively participated in all discussion segments. Demonstrated leadership awareness through her boot camp commander role.
JFP: Score 6/10 — Delivered a clear and reflective challenge presentation and contributed meaningfully to the thought-for-the-day discussion. However, repeated technical issues caused significant gaps in participation, and the boot camp update was underprepared.
BLC: Score 7/10 — Produced the most creatively sophisticated challenge presentation of the session, drawing on dream analysis and personal reflection. Asked intellectually strong questions and gave thoughtful responses. Slight deduction for hesitancy during the boot camp commitment discussion.
alwe (Ali): Score 5/10 — Showed genuine enthusiasm and creative thinking, particularly in chat contributions and the imaginative approach to the challenge. However, language barriers significantly limited verbal clarity, and the breathing exercise leadership required multiple corrections. Chat activity revealed higher engagement than verbal performance suggested.
Jayden: Score 5/10 — Participated actively during the emoji game and asked relevant questions during challenge Q&As. Verbal contributions during the main discussions were limited and sometimes unclear. Engagement was noticeably higher during interactive segments than during structured discussions.
BC (Ms. BCDF): Score 6/10 — Fulfilled her designated role as thought-for-the-day presenter effectively and facilitated a structured post-video discussion. Engagement was role-specific and did not extend significantly beyond her assigned segment.

Ali asked how long the exercise would be before beginning, which ELF addressed by redirecting him to start the exercise. SAHN's post-exercise feedback effectively addressed the gaps observed during the activity.
---
Weekly Challenge Presentations
The core of the session involved four members presenting their weekly challenges, all of which were centered on the theme of journaling. Each presenter shared their personal journaling experience, followed by a question-and-answer segment.
Key discussion points:
JFP's Presentation: JFP described completing the "Inner Explorer" challenge, which required writing three pages of unfiltered morning thoughts upon waking for three consecutive days. On day one, JFP's mind felt messy and scattered, filled with school-related worries and random thoughts. By day two, thoughts were more mixed but clearer, with some positive self-motivating ideas emerging. By day three, JFP reported feeling calmer, more organized, and more confident, with a shift from worry-based thinking to action-oriented planning. JFP concluded that journaling helped articulate thoughts more clearly and that treating it as a tool for self-improvement rather than a chore made it more sustainable.
Kyla's Presentation: Kyla also completed the "Inner Explorer" challenge and shared a summarized version of her morning pages. Her journal entry was written on her 15th birthday (April 3rd), capturing the excitement and mild panic of waking up at 5 AM to prepare for a birthday party she had only officially announced to friends the day before. Kyla described planning to make a matcha strawberry mille crepe cake and Japanese curry from her aunt's recipe, driven by a desire to serve something special made with love rather than something expensive. The entry also reflected on the passage of time, with Kyla noting that three years remained until she graduated and became an adult, and expressing a bittersweet nostalgia for childhood alongside excitement for the future.
BLC's Presentation: BLC took a unique approach to the challenge, writing three pages of morning pages based on a single vivid and surreal dream experienced the night before. The dream involved standing on a pier over a sea of liquid mercury, boarding a train that ran on a line of light, and finding the carriage filled with people BLC had lost contact with — all reading newspapers written in symbolic language. BLC sat next to an older version of themselves who handed them a warm stone. BLC's journaling process involved attempting to decode the dream's meaning, describing the sensory details of the dreamscape, and ultimately arriving at a personal reflection: the dream felt like a nudge to examine how BLC was handling personal growth, with the warm stone symbolizing the lessons carried from past experiences.
Ali's Presentation: Ali described a different approach to the challenge, writing about strange and imaginative thoughts that came to mind after waking up — inspired by content encountered on YouTube. Day one featured a scenario involving Socrates walking around Jogja (Yogyakarta); day two involved imagining what Marie Curie would be like if she were alive today; and day three featured Mario Bros becoming an F1 racer. Ali noted that this type of creative, unconstrained writing was enjoyable and that YouTube had suggested such exercises could enhance creativity.
Insights or decisions:
Across all four presentations, a consistent theme emerged: journaling — whether structured or free-form, dream-based or reality-based — consistently produced a sense of clarity, emotional relief, and self-awareness. The variety of approaches demonstrated that journaling is highly personal and adaptable, reinforcing ELF's earlier point that there is no single correct way to journal.
Questions addressed:
Multiple questions were raised during the Q&A segments following each presentation, which are documented in detail in Section 4.
---
Interactive Game: Guess the Country by Emoji (SAHN's Activity)
SAHN conducted a 10-minute interactive game in which participants were shown emoji combinations and asked to guess the corresponding country name. The activity served as an energy booster and a quick-thinking exercise.
Key discussion points:
The game covered a wide range of countries including Belgium, Germany, France, Poland, Iceland, China, Spain, Japan, Cuba, Finland, Thailand, Singapore, Ukraine, Oman, Portugal, Romania, Canada, Taiwan, Mali, Tonga, Denmark, Ireland, Greenland/Greece, Uruguay, Chile, Maldives, Sweden, Turkey, New Zealand, Kuwait, India, and Qatar. Participants competed enthusiastically to guess each answer, with BLC and Kyla emerging as particularly quick and accurate guessers. SAHN added an educational layer by occasionally asking for the capital cities of correctly identified countries, such as Helsinki for Finland, Ottawa for Canada, and Kyiv for Ukraine.
Insights or decisions:
The game was notably effective in raising the group's energy level and encouraging participation from members who had been quieter during the earlier segments. SAHN closed the activity by promising that similar games would be incorporated into future weekly sessions, which was met with enthusiasm from participants.
---
Thought for the Day: Story of "The Monkeys and the Bell"
Ms. BC (BCDF) presented a motivational video featuring an animated story called "The Monkeys and the Bell," framed within a conversation between two characters, Tia and Tofu, about overcoming fear.
Key discussion points:
The story followed a robber who stole a bell from a temple, only to be killed by a tiger attracted by the bell's sound. The bell was then found and played with by monkeys, causing villagers to believe an evil spirit was responsible. A brave woman investigated the truth, discovered the monkeys, lured them away with food, retrieved the bell, and was rewarded by the king. The moral of the story was that one must not be afraid of trifles, and that intelligence and courage succeed against all odds.
Insights or decisions:
Following the video, BC facilitated a structured discussion in which BLC, Kyla, Ali, Jayden, and JFP each contributed reflections. Kyla connected the story to her own experience of overcoming nervousness before a presentation, noting that she chose to proceed despite fear of judgment. JFP reflected that the story taught the importance of gathering facts before reacting to fear, and shared a personal anecdote about being afraid of crocodiles in a park before realizing trained guards were present. Ali summarized the lesson as "we cannot just say it straight away — we have to know the facts first." BLC reflected on the robber's story as a lesson in gratitude and contentment, arguing that greed and the desire for more than one already has can lead to negative consequences.
---
Boot Camp Updates and Announcements
In the final segment, ELF and members discussed upcoming boot camp activities and administrative updates.
Key discussion points:
ELF reminded all members who had not yet registered for the hybrid boot camp to do so as soon as possible. Kyla, who had been assigned as boot camp commander for her region, shared that she had already begun recruiting friends to participate and asked a clarifying question about the structure of Day 3 activities. JFP provided an overview of the planned boot camp structure: Day 1 would involve a community challenge in Singapore where participants would give muffins to elders and learn their stories; Day 2 would focus on innovation and creativity, imagining Singapore in 2040 and identifying personal traits and commitments; Day 3 would be a festival-style event with three games. ELF also announced that Ratna would be the host for the following week's session and that BLC had been assigned as the material provider for that session.
Insights or decisions:
BLC was asked directly whether they would attend the boot camp session that evening and gave an uncertain response, prompting ELF to request a clear yes or no reply via the group chat. ELF also reminded BLC to respond to messages and provide materials on time.

sessions.teaser: The group explored questioning through five-whys challenges, peer coaching, and a deep discussion on asking better questions.
sessions.fullSummary:
SECTION 1 — OVERVIEW
Meeting Objective: To conduct a structured team development session focused on the skill of questioning, including a scoreboard review, breathing exercise, challenge presentations, and a facilitated deep-dive discussion on the power of asking questions.
Total Meeting Duration: 47 minutes 48 seconds
Host / Facilitator: ELF (Session Host) | SAHN (Mentor/Supervisor)
Participant Roles:
- ELF — Session Host & Presenter
- SAHN — Mentor/Supervisor, Discussion Facilitator
- Jfp (Jeffrey/JFP) — Participant, Challenge Presenter, Breathing Exercise Leader
- alwe (Ali) — Participant, Challenge Presenter
Overall Engagement Level: Medium
Overall Sentiment: Mixed — predominantly positive with some neutral and directive moments
Notable Dynamics: SAHN dominated the latter half of the session with deep Socratic-style coaching, while ELF effectively managed the session structure. Ali and JFP showed willingness to engage but required significant prompting. Attendance was notably low, with several expected members absent.
Session Effectiveness Score: 6.5/10 — The session delivered meaningful coaching moments and practical application of the questioning concept, particularly through SAHN's guided discussions. However, low attendance, absent materials (thought for the day), and incomplete challenge execution by some members reduced overall effectiveness.
---
SECTION 2 — KEY DISCUSSIONS & TOPICS
Topic 1: Session Opening, Scoreboard Review & Emotional Landscape
ELF opened the session by introducing the topic of questioning, defining it as the practice of asking questions that help one understand their surroundings better, think beyond conventional thinking, and evaluate oneself. ELF outlined three challenges assigned to participants: (1) taking a current problem and asking "why" five times in succession, (2) asking someone well-known a question never previously asked, and (3) looking at a common object and asking what if it were designed for the opposite purpose.
Key discussion points:
ELF then presented the scoreboard, revealing that all members except Jayden had completed the challenge. ELF and Kyla shared the highest score of 7.7, followed by BL2P at 7.3, JFP at 6.9, Ali at 5.2, and Jayden at 4.7. ELF noted that as the host, their own score was equivalent to Kyla's. The emotional landscape data was also shared, indicating that 39.6% of the session's emotional tone was positive, 35.4% neutral, 8.3% somewhat mixed, and 16.7% directive. ELF expressed the aspiration to make the emotional landscape entirely positive going forward.
Insights or decisions:
Chart 3 was discussed, revealing that ELF asked the best quality questions and received the most questions, while Jayden asked the most questions but received the fewest. JFP was specifically called out to improve the quality of questions asked. ELF also encouraged participants to ask questions through the chat box in a timely manner.
Questions addressed:
No major questions were raised during this segment; it was primarily a data presentation by ELF.
---
Topic 2: Breathing Exercise
Before moving into the challenge presentations, ELF invited JFP to lead the group through a breathing exercise, a recurring weekly activity for the team.
Key discussion points:
JFP guided participants through a structured breathing exercise, instructing everyone to sit straight with feet on the ground to "connect with the energy of the earth." The exercise involved imagining a bubble inside the stomach that expands upon inhaling and contracts upon exhaling. JFP led the group through five rounds of breathing in for a count of five and breathing out for a count of five, creating a calm and grounded atmosphere before the challenge presentations began.
Insights or decisions:
The breathing exercise appeared to be a well-established ritual within the team's weekly sessions, suggesting a deliberate focus on mindfulness and emotional regulation as part of the team's development culture.
Questions addressed:
No questions were raised during this segment.
---
Topic 3: Ali's Challenge Presentation — Asking a Personal Question
Ali presented his challenge, which was to ask someone a question he had never asked before. Ali shared that he asked his friend Izar a personal question about what he feels when his family is mad at him. Ali noted that his friend's answer was casual and that he wanted to avoid causing long-term problems, so he chose to keep things positive with his family.
Key discussion points:
After Ali's presentation, JFP asked Ali whether he could answer the same question himself — specifically, what he would do or feel if his own family were mad at him. Ali responded that he would feel a little sad. JFP acknowledged the response and offered brief feedback. SAHN interjected to clarify whether Ali had finished asking his question, noting that what Ali offered was more of feedback than a formal question, prompting a brief clarification exchange between SAHN, JFP, and Ali.
Insights or decisions:
The exchange highlighted a subtle but important distinction between asking questions and offering feedback — a distinction that SAHN flagged as relevant to the session's learning objectives. Ali's challenge demonstrated a willingness to engage in personal inquiry, though the depth of the question and the follow-through were limited.
Questions addressed:
JFP asked Ali: "Can you answer the question you asked your friend — what do you do if your family is mad at you?" Ali responded that he would feel sad, which JFP accepted as a valid answer.
---
Topic 4: JFP's Challenge Presentation — The Five Whys on Nervousness
JFP presented his challenge, which involved applying the "Five Whys" root cause analysis technique to a personal problem. JFP chose the challenge of feeling nervous before important presentations.
Key discussion points:
JFP explained that he asked himself why he feels nervous before presentations and arrived at the answer that he is afraid of making mistakes. Asking why again, he realized it was because he cares deeply about how others perceive him. Continuing the chain, he found that others' opinions matter because he wants to be respected and thought well of. The final layer revealed that he sometimes judges his own self-worth based on how well he performs. JFP concluded that the nervousness was not just about presentations but about the internal pressure he places on himself to always perform well.
Insights or decisions:
Ali responded to JFP's presentation by offering the perspective that mistakes are normal and that one can always retry and improve. JFP acknowledged this as helpful advice. However, SAHN later pointed out that JFP's application of the Five Whys did not fully meet the exercise's objective, as JFP's answers tended to circle back to the same root cause rather than peeling back distinct layers of understanding.
Questions addressed:
Ali asked JFP: "You worry about making mistakes, but mistakes are normal — if you make a mistake, you can just retry and become good again." While framed as feedback rather than a question, it prompted JFP to affirm the lesson learned.
---
Topic 5: SAHN's Facilitated Discussion — Deepening the Five Whys with JFP
Following the challenge presentations, SAHN took the lead in facilitating a deeper, Socratic-style discussion with JFP to demonstrate the proper application of the Five Whys methodology.
Key discussion points:
SAHN used ELF's suggested scenario — what would you do if your life plans don't go as expected, using the example of wanting to become a professional footballer — to walk JFP through the questioning process step by step. JFP initially responded with practical answers such as looking for other job opportunities or trying again, but SAHN consistently pushed deeper, asking JFP to reflect on his emotional state first before jumping to solutions. JFP acknowledged he would feel sad but would overcome it and look for other aspirations. SAHN challenged this by asking whether JFP would even want to try again before giving up, and JFP agreed he would.
SAHN then guided JFP to identify the most important first question to ask himself in such a situation — not "can I try again?" but rather "where did I go wrong?" JFP eventually arrived at this insight, acknowledging that he would ask his coach, fellow players, and others for feedback. SAHN reinforced that asking questions at every step of problem-solving is the only way to truly learn and improve. SAHN used the analogy of peeling an onion — each layer of questioning reveals a deeper layer of understanding, and one cannot reach the core without peeling through each layer methodically.
Insights or decisions:
SAHN delivered a key insight: "Asking questions is our only way of learning." He further emphasized that even with abundant information from media and social networks, that information is useless if one does not ask questions about how to apply it. The discussion reinforced that the Five Whys technique requires genuine depth and distinct answers at each level, not circular reasoning.
Questions addressed:
SAHN asked JFP a series of progressively deeper questions, including: "What is your first reaction when your plan doesn't work out?", "How do you know what went wrong?", "How will you fix the concentration issue?", and "How do you know that doing more drills will help?" Each question was designed to model the kind of layered inquiry the Five Whys exercise was intended to develop.
---
Topic 6: SAHN's Facilitated Discussion — Deepening the Five Whys with Ali
SAHN then turned to Ali and applied the same Socratic coaching approach, using a real-life personal situation as the basis for the exercise.
Key discussion points:
SAHN prompted Ali to identify a recurring comment or situation in his life. Ali shared that both his parents frequently tell him not to argue, even though Ali himself does not feel he is arguing. Ali explained that he tends to go silent in these situations to avoid prolonging the conflict. SAHN explored this tension with Ali, acknowledging that both Ali and his father could be right or wrong, and that the only way to resolve the confusion is to ask questions.
SAHN guided Ali to consider asking his father directly: "Father, why do you think I am arguing?" Ali then offered his own hypothesis — that it might be because of his tone of voice, which tends to be slightly high. SAHN validated this as a possible reason but encouraged Ali to confirm it by asking rather than assuming. SAHN further walked Ali through the next layer of questioning: if the father confirms it is about the words Ali uses, then Ali should ask which specific words are problematic, and then after changing those words, if the father still perceives arguing, Ali should ask why again.
Insights or decisions:
SAHN concluded this segment with a powerful summary: "Only if you ask questions can you solve the problems you have, get more information, or get more clarity in your thought." He reinforced that the Five Whys technique is applicable not just in academic or professional settings but in everyday personal relationships. Ali confirmed that the exercise was very helpful.
Questions addressed:
SAHN asked Ali: "Did you ask your father why he thinks you are arguing?" and "Which words do you use that make your father think you are arguing?" — both of which Ali had not previously considered, highlighting the practical value of the questioning framework.
---
Topic 7: Session Closing & Next Week's Updates
ELF closed the session by thanking SAHN, JFP, and Ali for their participation and contributions. ELF provided a brief update on the following week's session.
Key discussion points:
ELF announced that the topic for the next session would be Research, and that BLCP would be responsible for preparing the materials. SECTION 3 — CHAT BOX SUMMARY
During the session, chat activity was minimal, with only one substantive message captured in the transcript. While the screen sharing text referenced several visual elements from the presentation slides — including labels such as "P2P questions Emotional," "Quality JEP," "Chart 2," "Chart 3," "Effort Spent," "Knowledge Application," and notes about bubble size representing question quality — these were part of the shared presentation materials rather than participant-generated chat messages.
The single notable chat message was posted by alwe (Ali) during the facilitated discussion between SAHN and JFP. The message read: "I feel like private lessons." This comment, while brief, was significant in capturing Ali's perception of the session dynamic at that moment. The Socratic back-and-forth between SAHN and JFP had become quite focused and individualized, resembling a one-on-one coaching or tutoring session rather than a group discussion. Ali's observation, though informal, reflected an honest and perceptive reading of the room — the session had temporarily shifted from a group learning format to what felt like a personalized mentoring exchange.
This comment also indirectly surfaced a potential structural concern: when the facilitator engages deeply with one participant for an extended period, other participants may feel sidelined or disengaged. Ali's message suggested he was still present and observant, but the comment implies he may not have felt actively included in that portion of the discussion. Notably, SAHN did subsequently pivot to engage Ali directly in a similar deep-dive exercise, which addressed this imbalance and ensured Ali also received individualized coaching.
The screen-sharing text fragments visible during ELF's presentation — referencing bubble charts, emotional landscapes, and quality metrics — indicate that the session made use of visual data tools to present participant performance. These visuals supported ELF's verbal summary of scores and emotional landscape percentages, providing a data-driven foundation for the session's reflective components. However, since these were presentation artifacts rather than chat contributions, they do not constitute substantive chat activity in the traditional sense.
Overall, the chat box was not actively used as a discussion or engagement tool during this session, which represents a missed opportunity for participants — particularly those who may have been more hesitant to speak verbally — to contribute questions, reactions, or reflections in real time.
---
SECTION 4 — QUESTIONS BY PARTICIPANT
SAHN (Mentor/Supervisor)
SAHN was by far the most prolific questioner in the session, using questions as the primary vehicle for coaching and deepening participants' understanding of the session's theme.
One of SAHN's most impactful early questions was directed at JFP: "Can you take us through the process of how you went through asking the same question five times?" This question was asked after JFP presented his Five Whys challenge, and it was designed to assess whether JFP had genuinely engaged with the methodology or had simply produced surface-level answers. JFP's response revealed that his answers had largely circled back to the same root cause, prompting SAHN to introduce the onion-peeling analogy and redirect the discussion toward a more practical demonstration.
SAHN followed this with: "Even five times, you got the same answer?" — a pointed question that gently challenged JFP to recognize that the exercise had not been fully executed as intended. This question was not confrontational but rather diagnostic, helping JFP understand the gap between what he did and what the methodology requires.
During the live coaching exercise with JFP using the footballer scenario, SAHN asked a series of progressively deeper questions. He began with "What is the emotion that you will have when you realize your plan is not going to happen?" — redirecting JFP away from practical problem-solving and toward emotional self-awareness, which is the necessary starting point for genuine root cause analysis. When JFP jumped to solutions, SAHN asked "But you wouldn't know in the first stance that it's gonna work again or not, right?" — a question that introduced nuance and uncertainty into JFP's thinking, encouraging him to sit with ambiguity rather than rushing to resolution.
SAHN's question "How do you know that doing more drills will help that issue?" was particularly powerful, as it challenged JFP to justify his proposed solution rather than accepting it at face value. This question modeled the kind of critical inquiry that the session was designed to cultivate, demonstrating that questioning is not just about identifying problems but also about scrutinizing proposed solutions.
With Ali, SAHN asked: "Did you ask your father why he thinks you are arguing?" This question was transformative in the context of Ali's situation, as it revealed that Ali had been operating on assumptions rather than direct inquiry. The question opened up a new avenue of understanding for Ali, who had previously only considered his own perspective. SAHN then asked: "Which words do you use that make your father think you are arguing?" — a question that pushed Ali to recognize that he did not actually know the specific trigger, reinforcing the necessity of asking rather than assuming.
SAHN's closing question to Ali — "If your father says it's because of the words you use, what is the next question you can ask him?" — was a masterful example of teaching through questioning, as it required Ali to generate the next layer of inquiry himself rather than receiving it from SAHN. This approach ensured that Ali internalized the methodology rather than simply observing it.
JFP (Jeffrey)
JFP asked one notable question during the session, directed at Ali during the challenge review segment. After Ali presented his challenge of asking a friend a personal question, JFP asked: "Can you answer this question yourself?" — specifically, whether Ali could respond to the same question he had posed to his friend about what one feels when their family is mad at them. This was a thoughtful and relevant question that turned the exercise inward, encouraging Ali to apply the same reflective inquiry to himself rather than only observing it in others. The question demonstrated JFP's understanding of the session's theme and his ability to engage constructively with a peer's work.
ELF (Session Host)
ELF contributed one substantive question during the facilitated discussion segment. When SAHN asked JFP to think of a question to use for the Five Whys demonstration, ELF offered: "What happens if what you really want to do in life does not go as planned?" — using the example of wanting to become a footballer. This question was thoughtful and personally relevant, providing a rich scenario for the coaching exercise that followed. It demonstrated ELF's ability to contribute meaningfully to the discussion even while managing the session's logistics.
alwe (Ali)
Ali asked one question during the session, directed at JFP after JFP's challenge presentation. Ali asked: "You worry about making mistakes, but mistakes are normal — if you have a mistake, you can just retry and become good again, right?" While this was framed more as a statement or piece of advice than a formal question, it reflected Ali's genuine engagement with JFP's challenge and his attempt to offer a constructive perspective. sessions.keyTopics:
Topic 1: Session Opening, Scoreboard Review & Emotional Landscape
ELF opened the session by introducing the topic of questioning, defining it as the practice of asking questions that help one understand their surroundings better, think beyond conventional thinking, and evaluate oneself. ELF outlined three challenges assigned to participants: (1) taking a current problem and asking "why" five times in succession, (2) asking someone well-known a question never previously asked, and (3) looking at a common object and asking what if it were designed for the opposite purpose.
Key discussion points:
ELF then presented the scoreboard, revealing that all members except Jayden had completed the challenge. ELF and Kyla shared the highest score of 7.7, followed by BL2P at 7.3, JFP at 6.9, Ali at 5.2, and Jayden at 4.7. ELF noted that as the host, their own score was equivalent to Kyla's. The emotional landscape data was also shared, indicating that 39.6% of the session's emotional tone was positive, 35.4% neutral, 8.3% somewhat mixed, and 16.7% directive. ELF expressed the aspiration to make the emotional landscape entirely positive going forward.
Insights or decisions:
Chart 3 was discussed, revealing that ELF asked the best quality questions and received the most questions, while Jayden asked the most questions but received the fewest. JFP was specifically called out to improve the quality of questions asked. ELF also encouraged participants to ask questions through the chat box in a timely manner.
Questions addressed:
No major questions were raised during this segment; it was primarily a data presentation by ELF.
---
Topic 2: Breathing Exercise
Before moving into the challenge presentations, ELF invited JFP to lead the group through a breathing exercise, a recurring weekly activity for the team.
Key discussion points:
JFP guided participants through a structured breathing exercise, instructing everyone to sit straight with feet on the ground to "connect with the energy of the earth." The exercise involved imagining a bubble inside the stomach that expands upon inhaling and contracts upon exhaling. JFP led the group through five rounds of breathing in for a count of five and breathing out for a count of five, creating a calm and grounded atmosphere before the challenge presentations began.
Insights or decisions:
The breathing exercise appeared to be a well-established ritual within the team's weekly sessions, suggesting a deliberate focus on mindfulness and emotional regulation as part of the team's development culture.
Questions addressed:
No questions were raised during this segment.
---
Topic 3: Ali's Challenge Presentation — Asking a Personal Question
Ali presented his challenge, which was to ask someone a question he had never asked before. Ali shared that he asked his friend Izar a personal question about what he feels when his family is mad at him. Ali noted that his friend's answer was casual and that he wanted to avoid causing long-term problems, so he chose to keep things positive with his family.
Key discussion points:
After Ali's presentation, JFP asked Ali whether he could answer the same question himself — specifically, what he would do or feel if his own family were mad at him. Ali responded that he would feel a little sad. JFP acknowledged the response and offered brief feedback. SAHN interjected to clarify whether Ali had finished asking his question, noting that what Ali offered was more of feedback than a formal question, prompting a brief clarification exchange between SAHN, JFP, and Ali.
Insights or decisions:
The exchange highlighted a subtle but important distinction between asking questions and offering feedback — a distinction that SAHN flagged as relevant to the session's learning objectives. Ali's challenge demonstrated a willingness to engage in personal inquiry, though the depth of the question and the follow-through were limited.
Questions addressed:
JFP asked Ali: "Can you answer the question you asked your friend — what do you do if your family is mad at you?" Ali responded that he would feel sad, which JFP accepted as a valid answer.
---
Topic 4: JFP's Challenge Presentation — The Five Whys on Nervousness
JFP presented his challenge, which involved applying the "Five Whys" root cause analysis technique to a personal problem. JFP chose the challenge of feeling nervous before important presentations.
Key discussion points:
JFP explained that he asked himself why he feels nervous before presentations and arrived at the answer that he is afraid of making mistakes. Asking why again, he realized it was because he cares deeply about how others perceive him. Continuing the chain, he found that others' opinions matter because he wants to be respected and thought well of. The final layer revealed that he sometimes judges his own self-worth based on how well he performs. JFP concluded that the nervousness was not just about presentations but about the internal pressure he places on himself to always perform well.
Insights or decisions:
Ali responded to JFP's presentation by offering the perspective that mistakes are normal and that one can always retry and improve. JFP acknowledged this as helpful advice. However, SAHN later pointed out that JFP's application of the Five Whys did not fully meet the exercise's objective, as JFP's answers tended to circle back to the same root cause rather than peeling back distinct layers of understanding.
Questions addressed:
Ali asked JFP: "You worry about making mistakes, but mistakes are normal — if you make a mistake, you can just retry and become good again." While framed as feedback rather than a question, it prompted JFP to affirm the lesson learned.
---
Topic 5: SAHN's Facilitated Discussion — Deepening the Five Whys with JFP
Following the challenge presentations, SAHN took the lead in facilitating a deeper, Socratic-style discussion with JFP to demonstrate the proper application of the Five Whys methodology.
Key discussion points:
SAHN used ELF's suggested scenario — what would you do if your life plans don't go as expected, using the example of wanting to become a professional footballer — to walk JFP through the questioning process step by step. JFP initially responded with practical answers such as looking for other job opportunities or trying again, but SAHN consistently pushed deeper, asking JFP to reflect on his emotional state first before jumping to solutions. JFP acknowledged he would feel sad but would overcome it and look for other aspirations. SAHN challenged this by asking whether JFP would even want to try again before giving up, and JFP agreed he would.
SAHN then guided JFP to identify the most important first question to ask himself in such a situation — not "can I try again?" but rather "where did I go wrong?" JFP eventually arrived at this insight, acknowledging that he would ask his coach, fellow players, and others for feedback. SAHN reinforced that asking questions at every step of problem-solving is the only way to truly learn and improve. SAHN used the analogy of peeling an onion — each layer of questioning reveals a deeper layer of understanding, and one cannot reach the core without peeling through each layer methodically.
Insights or decisions:
SAHN delivered a key insight: "Asking questions is our only way of learning." He further emphasized that even with abundant information from media and social networks, that information is useless if one does not ask questions about how to apply it. The discussion reinforced that the Five Whys technique requires genuine depth and distinct answers at each level, not circular reasoning.
Questions addressed:
SAHN asked JFP a series of progressively deeper questions, including: "What is your first reaction when your plan doesn't work out?", "How do you know what went wrong?", "How will you fix the concentration issue?", and "How do you know that doing more drills will help?" Each question was designed to model the kind of layered inquiry the Five Whys exercise was intended to develop.
---
Topic 6: SAHN's Facilitated Discussion — Deepening the Five Whys with Ali
SAHN then turned to Ali and applied the same Socratic coaching approach, using a real-life personal situation as the basis for the exercise.
Key discussion points:
SAHN prompted Ali to identify a recurring comment or situation in his life. Ali shared that both his parents frequently tell him not to argue, even though Ali himself does not feel he is arguing. Ali explained that he tends to go silent in these situations to avoid prolonging the conflict. SAHN explored this tension with Ali, acknowledging that both Ali and his father could be right or wrong, and that the only way to resolve the confusion is to ask questions.
SAHN guided Ali to consider asking his father directly: "Father, why do you think I am arguing?" Ali then offered his own hypothesis — that it might be because of his tone of voice, which tends to be slightly high. SAHN validated this as a possible reason but encouraged Ali to confirm it by asking rather than assuming. SAHN further walked Ali through the next layer of questioning: if the father confirms it is about the words Ali uses, then Ali should ask which specific words are problematic, and then after changing those words, if the father still perceives arguing, Ali should ask why again.
Insights or decisions:
SAHN concluded this segment with a powerful summary: "Only if you ask questions can you solve the problems you have, get more information, or get more clarity in your thought." He reinforced that the Five Whys technique is applicable not just in academic or professional settings but in everyday personal relationships. Ali confirmed that the exercise was very helpful.
Questions addressed:
SAHN asked Ali: "Did you ask your father why he thinks you are arguing?" and "Which words do you use that make your father think you are arguing?" — both of which Ali had not previously considered, highlighting the practical value of the questioning framework.
---
Topic 7: Session Closing & Next Week's Updates
ELF closed the session by thanking SAHN, JFP, and Ali for their participation and contributions. ELF provided a brief update on the following week's session.
Key discussion points:
ELF announced that the topic for the next session would be Research, and that BLCP would be responsible for preparing the materials. ELF mentioned that further details would be shared via the Telegram group chat. ELF also encouraged all participants to invite their friends to join future sessions, noting that some members had been invited but had not responded. Ali mentioned that he had tried to invite friends but received no replies, to which SAHN humorously tied back to the session's theme by encouraging Ali to keep asking "why" until he gets a good answer.
Insights or decisions:
The closing reinforced the session's theme in a light-hearted way, with SAHN's parting comment about continuing to ask "why, why, why" serving as both a practical reminder and a motivational send-off.
Questions addressed:
SAHN asked ELF: "What is the topic for next week?" ELF confirmed it would be Research.

Session Effectiveness Score: 5/10 — The session achieved its core learning objectives through student presentations and an engaging quiz, but was undermined by structural gaps including a missing mindfulness segment, absent thought-for-the-day, incomplete attendance, and a backup host who was unprepared in advance.
---
SECTION 2 — KEY DISCUSSIONS & TOPICS
Scoreboard Review and Session Performance Analysis
The session opened with JFP sharing the scoreboard, which reflected the current standing of participants in the Learning Space program. JFP reported that his own score stood at 7.4, ELF's at 6.5, and Ali's at 5.6. A notable concern was raised regarding a significant drop in the number of participants, which JFP attributed to the fact that a face-to-face boot camp had recently taken place in Bali, drawing some members away from the online session. However, JFP also acknowledged that other online members such as BLTOP were still absent and unaccounted for.
Key discussion points:
JFP formally declared the previous session a failed one, citing the topic of "questioning" and noting that only two peer-to-peer questions had been asked throughout that session — far below the expected threshold for a productive learning exchange. As a result, JFP indicated that a recovery plan had been requested to address the shortfall. This was a candid and transparent acknowledgment of underperformance, setting a tone of accountability for the current session.
Insights or decisions:
The scoreboard review highlighted that participation levels are being actively tracked and that session quality is evaluated against measurable criteria. The identification of a "failed session" due to insufficient peer questioning underscored the program's emphasis on interactive, dialogue-driven learning rather than passive content delivery.
Questions addressed:
DAV raised a question via chat asking "Why Kyla?" in reference to the scoreboard or participant list, though this was not elaborated upon verbally. ELF also noted that the team introduction had been forgotten at the start, prompting a brief correction.
---
Module Transition: From Leadership to Global Citizens
DAV interjected early in the session to highlight an important programmatic shift that had not yet been communicated to participants. He noted that the program had transitioned away from the leadership module into a new thematic season, and he directed ELF to explain this change to the group.
Key discussion points:
ELF explained that the leadership season had officially concluded and that the program was now entering a new season focused on "growing into global citizens." ELF described this new phase as one centered on learning to solve one's own problems, staying flexible, and persevering through daily experiences. The overarching goal, as articulated by ELF, was for participants to be able to apply leadership skills in small but meaningful ways within their everyday lives. This framing positioned the new module as a practical, applied extension of the leadership concepts previously studied.
Insights or decisions:
The transition to the global citizens theme represents a deliberate pedagogical shift from theoretical leadership concepts toward real-world application and personal development. This context was important for grounding the session's topic of "research" within a broader developmental framework.
Questions addressed:
No specific questions were raised about the module transition, though the announcement was acknowledged by Kyla and other participants.
---
Topic Introduction: Understanding Research
JFP introduced the session's core academic topic — research — and provided an initial explanation to the group. JFP articulated that while many people associate research with simply going online and searching for information, the true meaning of research involves asking questions, collecting information based on those questions, and learning something new as a result. JFP identified three core components of research: asking questions, collecting information, and deriving new knowledge. He also provided examples such as looking up facts for a project, asking people questions, and conducting experiments.
Key discussion points:
Following JFP's explanation, ELF facilitated a round of comprehension checks by asking each participant to share their own understanding of research. Kyla described research as "studying and diving deeper into a specific topic that you have not fully understood," emphasizing the idea of observation and exploration. Ali, who participated via chat and verbally, defined research as "a form or way for us to clarify and deepen something," though he struggled to elaborate clearly when prompted. ELF encouraged Ali to expand on his definition, and Ali eventually connected research to the idea of being affected by new information from various sources.
Insights or decisions:
The comprehension check revealed varying levels of conceptual clarity among participants. Kyla demonstrated a reasonably solid grasp of the concept, while Ali's articulation was less precise, suggesting a need for continued scaffolding. The exercise effectively surfaced the participants' prior understanding before moving into applied examples.
Questions addressed:
ELF asked each participant directly: "What is your understanding of research now?" This question served as a formative assessment tool to gauge comprehension before the challenge presentations began.
---
Bootcamp Reflections and Linking Research to Real Experience
DAV prompted the group to connect the concept of research to their recent experiences at the Bali bootcamp, asking participants to share what they had done and learned there, and to link those experiences back to the theme of research. This segment was intended to bridge theoretical understanding with lived experience.
Key discussion points:
Kyla shared that during the bootcamp, her team engaged with paper strip questions that required them to delve deeper into the meaning of leadership — specifically, what a servant leader means and how to overcome difficult situations. She described motivating inattentive team members and scaling up engagement during activities.
